case_analysis.focal_point: Whether Congress’s 2017 Mandatory Repatriation Tax (MRT), which attributes a corporation’s undistributed foreign earnings to U.S. shareholders and taxes them without a shareholder-level realization event, is a permissible “tax on incomes” under the Sixteenth Amendment (and thus need not be apportioned).
case_analysis.legal_provision: U.S. Const. amend. XVI (Sixteenth Amendment: “power to lay and collect taxes on incomes, from whatever source derived, without apportionment”).
case_analysis.petitioner_position: The Moores argue the MRT is unconstitutional because it taxes shareholders on corporate earnings they did not personally realize or receive; in their view, the original public meaning of “income” at the time of the Sixteenth Amendment was confined to realized gains (a receipt or severance from capital). They contend Supreme Court precedent—particularly Eisner v. Macomber and later cases—treats realization (in some form) as a constitutional requirement for an income tax, so Congress cannot redefine “income” to include unrealized or undistributed corporate earnings attributed to shareholders. Therefore, absent apportionment, the MRT exceeds Congress’s Sixteenth Amendment power.
case_analysis.respondent_position: The United States argues the MRT falls within Congress’s Sixteenth Amendment power because it is a tax on “incomes” and fits longstanding practice of taxing shareholders/owners on income earned through entities even if not distributed (i.e., attribution/pass-through concepts). The government maintains realization at the shareholder level is not a constitutional prerequisite for an income tax so long as there is income in the relevant sense (here, corporate earnings) and Congress may choose reasonable mechanisms for assigning that income to taxpayers. It further contends petitioners’ reading conflicts with constitutional text, congressional practice, and this Court’s precedent, and that the MRT is a one-time transitional measure tied to pre-2018 foreign earnings.

John Roberts.reasoning: Justice Thomas’s strongest point—that Macomber’s “received or drawn” language implies a constitutional shareholder-level realization requirement—deserves a direct answer: Macomber’s holding is best confined to the stock-dividend situation where nothing is severed and no underlying earnings are being taxed to anyone at that moment, and it cannot be transposed into a rigid constitutional rule that bars Congress from attributing already-realized earnings. As Justice Kagan and Justice Alito emphasize, the Horst/Bruun line undercuts any categorical insistence on personal cash receipt by recognizing realization through control, enjoyment, or assignment mechanisms, and here the earnings are undeniably realized at the corporate level before attribution occurs. Treating distribution as a constitutional prerequisite would, as Alito warns, constitutionalize an administrability line and destabilize settled anti-deferral/pass-through regimes without clear support in the Sixteenth Amendment’s text. On narrow grounds—limited to a one-time tax on prior, realized corporate earnings attributed to U.S. shareholders—I would uphold the MRT as an income tax not requiring apportionment.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts’s effort to cabin Macomber to stock dividends does not answer the constitutional question his framing assumes: whether the Sixteenth Amendment permits Congress to tax a shareholder on “income” the shareholder has not realized, received, or had the legal power to command for separate use. Horst and Bruun, invoked by Justice Kagan and Justice Alito, do not undermine that original meaning because they involve taxpayers who possessed realized income or exercised dominion over it and merely redirected or enjoyed it; they do not authorize Congress to treat a third party’s undistributed earnings as the shareholder’s income by legislative attribution alone. Nor does the Amendment’s phrase “from whatever source derived” eliminate the distinction between taxing an entity’s realized gains and imposing a levy on the shareholder’s ownership interest measured by undistributed earnings—effectively a direct tax on property requiring apportionment. Administrability and longevity of pass-through regimes, emphasized by Roberts and others, cannot supply constitutional meaning or validate a statute that collapses the original public distinction between “income” and property-based burdens.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Justice Thomas’s best point remains his reading of Eisner v. Macomber as constitutionalizing a taxpayer-level “received or drawn” realization requirement, but I agree with Chief Justice Roberts that Macomber is properly confined to the pro rata stock-dividend setting where nothing was severed and no underlying earnings were being taxed as such. The Helvering v. Horst and Helvering v. Bruun line, emphasized by Roberts and Justice Kagan, matters because it shows our doctrine has treated “realization” as functional—turning on consummated economic gain and control/enjoyment—not a rigid rule that the same taxpayer must receive cash before Congress may tax. The MRT is keyed to corporate earnings that were in fact realized, and Congress’s attribution to U.S. shareholders resembles long-accepted anti-deferral/pass-through mechanisms rather than a disguised property tax on mere ownership; adopting Thomas’s broader constitutional rule would needlessly destabilize those regimes without clear textual support in the Sixteenth Amendment.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Justice Thomas’s strongest contention—that the Sixteenth Amendment requires shareholder-level “receipt” and that attribution of undistributed corporate earnings is therefore a forbidden direct tax—still overreads Eisner v. Macomber by treating its stock-dividend-specific severance language as a freestanding constitutional rule. As Justice Kagan and the Chief Justice note, Helvering v. Horst undermines a categorical personal-receipt requirement by recognizing taxable realization through control/assignment principles, which makes Congress’s use of attribution here look like an administrable anti-deferral mechanism rather than a property tax on stock ownership. I also agree with Justice Alito that constitutionalizing a distribution prerequisite would destabilize long-accepted pass-through and anti-deferral regimes and, as a practical matter, impair revenue and enforcement in ways that fall hardest on communities that rely on effective tax administration and public services. Nothing in the Sixteenth Amendment’s text compels Thomas’s rigid line, and the MRT targets actual earnings realized at the corporate level—income in the ordinary sense—even if Congress chose to tax it at the shareholder level to prevent deferral.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Justice Thomas’s strongest point remains that Macomber’s “received or drawn” language suggests a taxpayer-level realization requirement, and that Horst involved only the assignment of income already “owned” by the taxpayer. But I agree with Chief Justice Roberts that Macomber is best read as addressing the stock-dividend scenario where nothing was severed from the shareholder’s capital interest, while here there is real earnings realization at the corporate level and Congress is using attribution to identify the taxpayer rather than taxing mere ownership as such. Horst matters because it rejects the notion that personal cash receipt is the constitutional touchstone; realization can track control/enjoyment and administrable attribution principles, which fits longstanding anti-deferral regimes. Textually, the Sixteenth Amendment’s broad grant to tax “incomes, from whatever source derived” does not compel the rigid shareholder-receipt rule petitioner proposes, and adopting it would constitutionalize an administrability line in a way our later doctrine and the tax system have not recognized.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Justice Thomas’s best point is that Eisner v. Macomber spoke of income as something “received or drawn” by the taxpayer, but that language cannot be lifted from Macomber’s stock-dividend setting to constitutionalize a rigid, shareholder-level receipt requirement the Sixteenth Amendment’s text (“incomes, from whatever source derived”) does not contain. As Chief Justice Roberts emphasizes, the MRT is pegged to earnings actually realized at the corporate level, and Congress’s choice to attribute that realized income to U.S. shareholders resembles familiar anti-deferral and pass-through assignments rather than a tax on mere ownership. Thomas argues Helvering v. Horst is inapposite because it involves redirecting already-realized income, but Horst still undermines the categorical claim that personal cash receipt is constitutionally required for “realization,” recognizing instead that control and disposition principles can fix taxable income. Absent a clear textual/original-meaning command requiring apportionment whenever Congress uses attribution rather than waiting for distributions, I do not see a constitutional basis to strike this tax.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Justice Thomas’s best point remains that Macomber spoke in taxpayer-centered terms (“received or drawn”), and that the Horst line involves taxpayers who already had command of realized income. But I agree with Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Alito that Macomber should be confined to its stock-dividend context (no severance from capital), and that the MRT instead targets corporate earnings that were in fact realized—plainly “income”—with attribution serving as a familiar mechanism to identify the U.S. taxpayer in anti-deferral regimes. Thomas’s attempt to recast this as a direct tax on stock ownership is weakened by our subsequent cases’ functional treatment of realization (including Horst/Bruun) and by the long historical practice of taxing owners on entity-level realized income without apportionment. Given the absence of any explicit realization-at-the-shareholder requirement in the Sixteenth Amendment’s text and the destabilizing consequences of constitutionalizing Thomas’s broader reading, I would uphold the MRT on narrow, institutionally cautious grounds.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Justice Thomas’s strongest contention is that Macomber constitutionalizes a taxpayer-level “received” requirement, so that attribution of undistributed corporate earnings cannot qualify as “income” to the shareholder. But Macomber’s text and logic are tethered to the pro rata stock-dividend circumstance where no gain was separated from capital at all; it does not follow that Congress lacks power to tax actual earnings realized at the entity level and then assign that realized income to owners for taxation. Chief Justice Roberts’s reliance on Helvering v. Horst matters because it undercuts a rigid receipt rule by treating realization as capable of occurring through control/enjoyment and assignment principles, which makes Thomas’s distinction (entity taxed vs. shareholder taxed) less constitutionally categorical than he asserts. Given the Sixteenth Amendment’s broad language (“incomes, from whatever source derived”) and the long-accepted use of attribution in anti-deferral regimes, I do not see an original public meaning basis to convert Macomber’s stock-dividend holding into a general apportionment constraint here.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Justice Thomas’s severance/receipt framing from Eisner v. Macomber is the most serious objection, but I agree with Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan that Macomber’s language is best confined to its pro rata stock-dividend context and cannot be constitutionalized into a categorical shareholder-level realization prerequisite untethered from the Sixteenth Amendment’s text. Thomas’s attempt to cabin Helvering v. Horst to cases where the taxpayer already “possesses” realized income does not persuade me because Horst’s core insight is functional: realization can be fixed by control/enjoyment and attribution principles rather than literal personal cash receipt, and here Congress is taxing earnings that were in fact realized at the corporate level. Under a pragmatic, consequence-attentive approach, treating distribution as constitutionally mandatory would convert administrability lines into constitutional barriers and risk destabilizing settled anti-deferral and pass-through regimes without a clear constitutional command. I therefore continue to see the MRT as an income tax measured by real earnings with an attribution mechanism, not a direct tax on mere property ownership requiring apportionment.

John Roberts.reasoning: The MRT is best understood as a tax on “incomes” within the meaning of the Sixteenth Amendment because it taxes corporate earnings that have been realized at the entity level and then attributed to U.S. shareholders as a permissible allocation mechanism. Eisner v. Macomber’s realization language was tied to the distinct problem of stock dividends and was later treated as limited in scope rather than a broad constitutional prohibition on attribution regimes. Helvering v. Horst confirms that “income is not taxable until realized,” but also that realization may occur through control and assignment rather than personal receipt, undermining any categorical requirement of shareholder-level distribution. Given longstanding practice of taxing owners on entity income and the need for a narrow ruling that preserves institutional stability, I would uphold the MRT as within Congress’s Sixteenth Amendment power and not subject to apportionment.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: The Sixteenth Amendment authorizes unapportioned taxes only on “incomes,” and the original public meaning of that term, as reflected in this Court’s interpretation, requires a realized gain—something “received or drawn by the recipient for his separate use, benefit and disposal.” Eisner v. Macomber, 252 U.S. 189, 207–08 (1920). The MRT taxes U.S. shareholders on a corporation’s undistributed foreign earnings without a shareholder-level realization event, effectively treating mere attribution as “income” to the shareholder, which the constitutional text does not permit. Because this is not an “income” tax within the meaning of U.S. Const. amend. XVI, it is a direct tax requiring apportionment under Article I, and Congress cannot evade that limit by redefining “income” to include unrealized, undistributed corporate earnings.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: The Sixteenth Amendment authorizes Congress to “lay and collect taxes on incomes, from whatever source derived, without apportionment,” and the MRT taxes corporate earnings that are plainly “income” in the ordinary sense even if Congress attributes that income to U.S. shareholders rather than waiting for a distribution. Eisner v. Macomber’s realization language has been confined to the peculiar context of pro rata stock dividends, and subsequent cases treated “realization” as a matter of administrative and statutory line-drawing rather than a constitutional prerequisite (Helvering v. Horst; Helvering v. Bruun). Given longstanding acceptance of attribution/pass-through taxation and the significant practical consequences of disabling Congress from addressing accumulated foreign earnings, I would uphold the MRT as a permissible income tax not requiring apportionment under the Sixteenth Amendment. Macomber does not supply a broad constitutional rule that would invalidate this transitional regime.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: The Sixteenth Amendment authorizes Congress to tax “incomes, from whatever source derived” without apportionment, and the MRT functions as an income tax on corporate earnings by attributing those earnings to U.S. shareholders under a long-used anti-deferral approach. Eisner v. Macomber’s realization language arose in the narrow context of stock dividends that “brought about no change whatever” in the shareholder’s interest, and later cases limited Macomber rather than constitutionalizing a rigid, shareholder-level realization requirement for all income taxes. As a practical matter, accepting petitioners’ theory would destabilize longstanding pass-through/attribution regimes and impair Congress’s ability to prevent offshore income-shifting, with significant fairness costs and reduced fiscal capacity to fund protections for vulnerable communities. Because the MRT taxes income (corporate earnings) and uses a reasonable attribution mechanism, it fits within the Sixteenth Amendment and need not be apportioned.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: The Sixteenth Amendment authorizes unapportioned taxes on “incomes, from whatever source derived,” and the MRT taxes corporate earnings (income) using an attribution mechanism to U.S. shareholders rather than taxing mere ownership of stock as property. This Court has treated “realization” as largely a doctrine of administrative convenience, not a constitutional prerequisite, explaining in Helvering v. Horst that income may be taxed when “enjoyment is consummated by some event other than the taxpayer’s personal receipt of money or property.” Macomber’s narrow holding about a true stock dividend does not constitutionalize a shareholder-level receipt requirement in the face of longstanding pass-through/attribution taxation (e.g., partnership taxation) and Congress’s pragmatic need for workable rules for previously untaxed foreign earnings. Given statutory coherence and workability, the MRT fits within the Sixteenth Amendment as a tax on income and therefore need not be apportioned.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: The Sixteenth Amendment authorizes unapportioned taxes on “incomes, from whatever source derived,” and the MRT taxes income the corporation in fact earned; Congress’s choice to attribute those undistributed earnings to U.S. shareholders is a permissible assignment mechanism long familiar in pass-through and anti-deferral regimes. Eisner v. Macomber held only that a pro rata stock dividend was not “income” because it involved no gain severed from capital, but it does not establish a freestanding constitutional rule that realization must occur at the particular taxpayer level Congress selects. Read in light of the Amendment’s text and the Constitution’s separation of powers, it is not this Court’s role to constitutionalize a rigid realization requirement that the text does not contain, especially where the tax is measured by actual earnings and operates as a one-time transitional income tax rather than a tax on mere asset appreciation. Accordingly, the MRT fits within the Sixteenth Amendment’s grant and need not be apportioned.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: The MRT is a permissible “tax on incomes” under the Sixteenth Amendment because it taxes corporate earnings that have been realized at the entity level and Congress may reasonably attribute that income to U.S. shareholders under long-established anti-deferral and pass-through/attribution principles. Eisner v. Macomber is best read narrowly as a stock-dividend case involving no change in the shareholder’s proportionate interest and has been limited by later decisions that recognize Congress’s flexibility to tax income through assignment/attribution doctrines rather than requiring shareholder-level receipt. This Court’s post-Macomber cases, including Helvering v. Horst and Helvering v. Bruun, reflect that “realization” is not an inexorable constitutional prerequisite in all contexts, especially where there is an accession to wealth and Congress is addressing practical workability in the tax system. Given longstanding congressional practice in taxing U.S. owners on undistributed entity earnings and the serious destabilizing consequences of petitioners’ theory for the tax code, precedent, history, and institutional considerations counsel upholding the MRT as an unapportioned income tax.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: The Sixteenth Amendment authorizes taxes on “incomes, from whatever source derived,” and the MRT taxes corporate earnings—undeniably “income” at the entity level—while using an attribution mechanism to assign that income to U.S. shareholders. Eisner v. Macomber, 252 U.S. 189 (1920), is best read as addressing whether a pro rata stock dividend is itself “income” to the shareholder; its realization/severance language does not establish a categorical constitutional rule forbidding Congress from taxing undistributed but earned business income via ownership attribution. Consistent with Congress’s longstanding use of pass-through and anti-deferral regimes, the MRT fits within the original public meaning of “tax on incomes” and does not require apportionment under U.S. Const. amend. XVI. Respect for precedent and methodological consistency counsel against extending Macomber to invalidate broad swaths of entity-attribution taxation that this Court has not treated as constitutionally suspect.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: The Sixteenth Amendment authorizes Congress to tax “incomes, from whatever source derived, without apportionment,” and the MRT operates as an attribution mechanism taxing U.S. shareholders on corporate earnings that were realized at the corporate level, even if not distributed. Eisner v. Macomber’s realization language arose in the narrow context of a pro rata stock dividend and has been treated as fact-bound rather than a categorical constitutional bar to Congress assigning entity-level realized income to owners under anti-deferral regimes. Given longstanding practice of pass-through and attribution taxation and the practical consequences of disabling Congress from addressing offshore deferral through transitional measures, I would uphold the MRT as a permissible income tax under the Sixteenth Amendment without apportionment.

case_analysis.focal_point: Whether Congress’s Mandatory Repatriation Tax (MRT), which attributes a U.S. shareholder’s share of a foreign corporation’s accumulated earnings and taxes that amount without a contemporaneous distribution, is a constitutionally permissible "tax[] on incomes" under the Sixteenth Amendment (and thus need not be apportioned).
case_analysis.legal_provision: U.S. Const. amend. XVI (Sixteenth Amendment: "taxes on incomes, from whatever source derived, without apportionment"); the underlying federal statute discussed in the case materials is the Mandatory Repatriation Tax enacted in the Tax Cuts and Jobs Act of 2017 (an Internal Revenue Code provision taxing deemed repatriation of certain foreign earnings).
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Petitioners contend the MRT is unconstitutional because it taxes shareholders on amounts they did not actually receive—i.e., it reaches unrealized/unreceived gains or earnings—and thus exceeds the Sixteenth Amendment’s authorization to tax "incomes." Relying on ratification-era meaning and Supreme Court precedent (particularly Eisner v. Macomber), they argue "income" historically required realization (receipt of an economic benefit in a realized form), so Congress cannot redefine income to include unrealized gains or undistributed corporate earnings; if not an "income" tax, the MRT would be a direct tax requiring apportionment.
case_analysis.respondent_position: The United States argues the MRT fits comfortably within Congress’s Sixteenth Amendment power to tax incomes without apportionment and is consistent with longstanding congressional practice and Supreme Court doctrine permitting taxation of certain income allocations/attributions without a cash distribution. It maintains petitioners’ realization-based theory is overbroad, conflicts with the constitutional text and history, and would destabilize major portions of the tax code; additionally, as framed in the opposition materials, the MRT’s one-time, backward-looking character also reduces the need for Supreme Court review.

John Roberts.reasoning: Justice Thomas’s objection usefully clarifies the line he wants: Horst as mere assignment-of-income versus an impermissible legislative attribution of a corporation’s retained earnings to shareholders. But Macomber’s “severance/receipt” language is best confined to its stock-dividend context, and, as Justice Kavanaugh notes, Horst’s treatment of realization as an administrability concept undercuts converting that dictum into a rigid constitutional receipt requirement. The MRT targets earnings that have been realized at the corporate level and then included to shareholders via a longstanding anti-deferral attribution mechanism—closer in kind to accepted pass-through and anti-avoidance regimes than to a tax on mere unrealized appreciation—so Thomas’s apportionment theory asks us to unsettle large swaths of settled taxation without clear textual command in “incomes, from whatever source derived.” I therefore favor a narrow holding upholding the MRT on attribution/realization-at-the-entity-level grounds while expressly reserving the constitutionality of taxes on unrealized appreciation untethered to any realization event.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kavanaugh rely on Helvering v. Horst to argue that realization is merely administrability and that “enjoyment” can be consummated without receipt, but Horst involved a taxpayer’s own income right that he controlled and assigned—an application of the longstanding rule that one cannot avoid tax on income one has realized by redirecting it. That precedent does not establish Congress’s power under the Sixteenth Amendment to deem a distinct corporation’s undistributed earnings to be the shareholder’s “income” absent any distribution or shareholder-level severance from capital, which is what Eisner v. Macomber’s original-meaning account of “income” captures. Justice Gorsuch’s “entity-level realization” point explains why Congress may tax the corporation on realized earnings, but it does not answer the constitutional question here: whether the shareholder has an unapportioned-income-taxable accession when nothing has come in to him. The colleagues’ appeal to disruption and workability cannot override the Amendment’s original public meaning; if the MRT is a direct tax on ownership measured by retained earnings, apportionment is required.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Justice Thomas’s best point remains that “income” at ratification was commonly understood as something “received” by the taxpayer, and that Helvering v. Horst involved a taxpayer redirecting income he had a right to receive rather than Congress attributing a corporation’s undistributed earnings to shareholders. But as Chief Justice Roberts stresses, Macomber’s severance/realization language has been cabined to its stock-dividend context, and Horst’s broader teaching—that Congress may tax when economic gain has been fixed and enjoyed through legally significant events even without cash in hand—undercuts any rigid constitutional receipt rule. The MRT targets earnings actually realized at the entity level and then includes them via a long-accepted attribution/anti-deferral mechanism, so treating it as an unapportioned income tax fits the Sixteenth Amendment’s text (“from whatever source derived”) and avoids the serious practical disruptions to settled regimes that Thomas’s apportionment theory would invite. Under a textualist approach attentive to administrability and precedent, I do not see a clear constitutional command requiring shareholder-level distribution as a prerequisite to taxation here.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Justice Thomas’s strongest point—that the Sixteenth Amendment’s original meaning requires shareholder-level receipt and that Eisner v. Macomber constitutionalizes a severance/receipt rule—still reads Macomber far beyond its narrow stock-dividend setting and would freeze a tax-administration concept into a constitutional barrier. Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan persuasively invoke Helvering v. Horst to show our cases do not demand personal cash-in-hand when Congress taxes an economically fixed gain through a legally significant event, and here the gain was already realized at the corporate level and permissibly attributed to owners to prevent deferral. Even accepting Thomas’s entity/attribution distinction, Congress has long treated owners as the relevant tax subjects for certain entity earnings, and striking that down would predictably shift burdens onto wage earners and weaken revenue stability—real-world consequences that matter when the text (“from whatever source derived”) does not clearly compel Thomas’s rigid receipt rule. No colleague has identified a precedent that squarely makes shareholder-level distribution a constitutional prerequisite outside Macomber’s peculiar facts, so I remain with the Respondent.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Justice Thomas’s best point is that Helvering v. Horst involved assignment of income the taxpayer had a right to receive, and he argues that deemed attribution of undistributed corporate earnings is constitutionally different. But the Sixteenth Amendment’s text—“taxes on incomes, from whatever source derived”—does not embed a shareholder-level receipt requirement, and (as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kavanaugh emphasize) Macomber’s severance language has been confined to its stock-dividend setting rather than treated as a free-standing constitutional rule. Here the earnings were actually realized at the corporate level and Congress’s attribution rule is a workable, longstanding anti-deferral mechanism; treating “realization/receipt” as a constitutional prerequisite would create major statutory incoherence without a clear textual command. Thomas’s distinction is not trivial, but under a pragmatic textualist approach it is not enough to reclassify this as an unapportioned direct tax.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Justice Thomas is right to insist Horst cannot do all the work here because it involved assignment of income the taxpayer otherwise had a legal right to receive, not Congress attributing a corporation’s retained earnings to shareholders. But Macomber’s “severance/receipt” language arose in the peculiar stock-dividend setting and, as Chief Justice Roberts emphasizes, our subsequent cases have not treated shareholder-level receipt as a constitutional prerequisite so much as an administrability convention—especially where Congress targets income that is actually earned and fixed at an entity level. On a textual and original public meaning reading of “taxes on incomes, from whatever source derived,” I do not see a clear constitutional command that forbids Congress from using longstanding attribution rules to tax realized corporate earnings to U.S. owners to prevent deferral. Thomas’s approach would constitutionalize a distribution requirement that neither the Sixteenth Amendment’s broad text nor our post-Macomber precedent compels, and it would unsettle entrenched anti-deferral/pass-through features without necessity.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Justice Thomas’s key point—that “income” originally required shareholder-level receipt and that Congress cannot attribute a corporation’s undistributed earnings to the shareholder—does not overcome the combined force of our precedent and institutional practice. As Chief Justice Roberts emphasizes, Eisner v. Macomber has long been confined to the stock-dividend setting, and Helvering v. Horst undercuts any attempt to constitutionalize a rigid personal-receipt rule by treating “realization” as largely an administrability concept where legally significant events can fix taxable gain without cash in hand. The MRT targets earnings actually realized at the corporate level and uses a familiar anti-deferral attribution mechanism akin in principle to pass-through taxation, making Thomas’s entity/separateness distinction insufficient to convert this into a constitutionally “direct tax” requiring apportionment. Given the Sixteenth Amendment’s broad text and the destabilizing consequences of Thomas’s theory for entrenched attribution regimes, I remain persuaded the MRT is permissible without apportionment.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Justice Thomas’s core objection—that the Sixteenth Amendment’s original public meaning constitutionalizes a shareholder-level receipt requirement—leans too heavily on Eisner v. Macomber’s severance language, which arose in a narrow stock-dividend setting and has not been treated as a general constitutional limit. Chief Justice Roberts’s reliance on Helvering v. Horst matters because it confirms that personal cash receipt is not the touchstone where Congress taxes a concrete accession to wealth through attribution rules; the MRT targets earnings already realized at the entity level and assigns them to U.S. shareholders by statute. Even accepting Thomas’s point that Horst involved redirected income the taxpayer had a right to receive, the broader principle it reflects—realization as an administrable construct rather than a rigid constitutional prerequisite—undercuts importing Macomber’s dictum to invalidate longstanding anti-deferral regimes. Textually, “taxes on incomes, from whatever source derived” does not compel a distribution requirement, and reading one into the Amendment would destabilize settled attribution systems without clear constitutional warrant.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Justice Thomas’s best point is the constitutional attribution objection—that Helvering v. Horst involved redirecting income the taxpayer was already entitled to receive, while the MRT taxes undistributed corporate earnings that never "came in" to the shareholder. But as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan emphasize, our post-Macomber cases treat “realization” chiefly as an administrability concept, and the constitutionally relevant event is the fixing of an economic gain through legally significant rules, not cash receipt; here, the gain was realized at the entity level and Congress attributed it to owners under a familiar anti-deferral design. Macomber’s severance language, read in context, cannot bear the weight Thomas places on it without destabilizing longstanding pass-through and deemed-inclusion regimes—an outcome not compelled by the Sixteenth Amendment’s broad “from whatever source derived” text. Under a pragmatic, consequences-aware approach attentive to procedural fairness and workability, Thomas’s theory would convert a narrow stock-dividend holding into a sweeping constitutional limit with serious systemic disruption and no clear textual mandate.

John Roberts.reasoning: The MRT is best sustained as a "tax[] on incomes" within the Sixteenth Amendment because it taxes U.S. shareholders on their pro rata share of a foreign corporation’s accumulated earnings—an attribution approach Congress has long employed—and this Court has rejected the view that realization by personal receipt is a constitutional prerequisite. Helvering v. Horst explained that the realization rule is largely one of administrative convenience and that enjoyment of economic benefit may be "consummated by some event other than the taxpayer’s personal receipt of money or property," undercutting petitioners’ broad reading of Eisner v. Macomber. Given that Macomber has been confined in later cases and that invalidating the MRT would cast doubt on settled attribution regimes, a narrow, institution-preserving ruling upholding the MRT is warranted rather than constitutionalizing a rigid realization requirement.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: The Sixteenth Amendment permits unapportioned "taxes on incomes," and the original public meaning of "income" at ratification was commonly understood to require realization—something that "comes in" or is "received"—rather than mere paper gains or undistributed corporate accumulations. Eisner v. Macomber, 252 U.S. 189 (1920), adopted that understanding, holding that mere appreciation or non-received accretions are not "income" within the Amendment’s meaning, and Merchants’ Loan & Trust Co. v. Smietanka, 255 U.S. 509, 519 (1921), described Macomber as reflecting what the people understood when adopting the Amendment. Because the MRT (Tax Cuts and Jobs Act of 2017) taxes U.S. shareholders on attributed, undistributed foreign earnings without a contemporaneous distribution, it exceeds the Sixteenth Amendment’s income-tax authorization; absent that authorization, it operates as a direct tax that would require apportionment.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: The Sixteenth Amendment authorizes “taxes on incomes, from whatever source derived,” and Congress may tax income when it is earned by the entity and attributed to the shareholder under a valid accounting regime, even absent a contemporaneous cash distribution. Eisner v. Macomber’s realization discussion arose in the narrow context of pro rata stock dividends and does not establish a broad constitutional prohibition on attributing undistributed corporate earnings to owners; later doctrine has treated “income” more capaciously, focusing on undeniable accessions to wealth within Congress’s chosen tax system rather than formal receipt. The MRT operates as a one-time transition measure taxing previously accumulated earnings of controlled foreign corporations that Congress could have taxed currently under anti-deferral regimes, and invalidating it would threaten significant, longstanding portions of the Code that rely on attribution principles. Given the text’s breadth and the practical consequences for federal revenue and administrability, I would uphold the MRT as a permissible tax on incomes not requiring apportionment.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: The MRT is a constitutionally permissible “tax[] on incomes” under the Sixteenth Amendment because it taxes a U.S. shareholder on their pro rata share of a corporation’s accumulated earnings—i.e., actual economic gains realized at the corporate level—through a long-accepted attribution mechanism, even absent a contemporaneous cash distribution. Eisner v. Macomber does not compel a rigid constitutional “realization” rule here; later decisions quickly confined Macomber’s reach and recognized that Congress may tax shareholders on corporate earnings when the law treats those earnings as severed for the shareholder’s benefit in a meaningful sense (see United States v. Phellis and Rockefeller v. United States).
